Analysis of Variance Tables

Source: vignettes/articles/anova.qmd 
library(dplyr)
library(apa7)
library(afex)
library(car)
library(ggplot2)
my_font <- "Roboto Condensed"
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)

The apa_anova function makes APA-style analysis of variance (ANOVA) source tables. Like apa_parameters, it relies on the easystats packages to do the computing: parameters::model_parameters gets the sums of squares, F tests, and p-values, and the effectsize package computes effect sizes and their confidence intervals. The workflow is the same as for regression tables:

  1. Fit a model with aov, lm, one of the afex functions (aov_car, aov_ez, or aov_4), or lme4::lmer.
  2. apa_anova converts the fit object into a tibble.
  3. In Quarto and R Markdown documents, the tibble is displayed as an APA-style table automatically. Pass it to apa_flextable to customize the table or save it.

apa_anova accepts:

Object Example
Between-subjects models aov(y ~ a * b, data), lm(y ~ a * b, data)
Repeated-measures models with error strata aov(y ~ a * b + Error(id / b), data)
afex models afex::aov_ez("id", "y", data, between = "a", within = "b")
Linear mixed models lme4::lmer(y ~ a * b + (1 | id), data), lmerTest::lmer(...)
ANOVA tables anova(fit), car::Anova(fit, type = 2), anova(lmerTest_fit)

Between-Subjects Designs

A one-way design

In the Friendly data set from the carData package (Friendly & Franklin, 1980), 30 participants learned a list of 40 words over several trials, 10 in each of three presentation formats: standard free recall, a format in which the words a participant had already recalled were presented before the other words, and a format in which they were mixed in with the other words. Does the number of words recalled on the final trial differ by presentation format?

d_recall <- carData::Friendly |>
  mutate(
    condition = factor(
      condition,
      levels = c("SFR", "Before", "Meshed"),
      labels = c("Standard", "Recalled Words First", "Recalled Words Mixed In")
    )
  ) |>
  rename(
    `Presentation Format` = condition,
    `Words Recalled` = correct
  )

fit_recall <- aov(`Words Recalled` ~ `Presentation Format`, data = d_recall)
Code
d_recall |> 
  ggplot(aes(`Presentation Format`, `Words Recalled`, color = `Presentation Format`)) + 
  # geom_violin() +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, position = position_nudge(.1)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "text", aes(label = after_stat(y)), position = position_nudge(.15), hjust = 0, family = my_font) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(alpha = .5, pch = 16) + 
  theme_minimal(base_family = my_font, base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(begin = .2, end = .7)
Warning: Computation failed in `stat_summary()`.
Caused by error in `fun.data()`:
! The package "Hmisc" is required.
apa_anova(fit_recall)

The table has a row for each effect and a row for the error term (the residuals). Its columns are the sums of squares (SS), degrees of freedom (df), mean squares (MS), the F test with its p-value, and eta squared (η2). The default effect size is partial η2, but in a one-way design, partial and non-partial η2 are the same, so the column is labeled η2.

In the console, apa_anova prints as an ordinary tibble, so you can inspect it or post-process it with dplyr. Here as_tibble is used to show that tibble in this document.

In follow-up tests using apa_contrast, we can see that performance was lower in the standard condition, compared to the other conditions, which had equal means:

apa_contrasts(fit_recall, 
              contrast = `Presentation Format`, 
              p_adjust = "tukey",
              effect_size = FALSE) |> 
  mutate(`Presentation Format` = stringr::str_remove(
    `Presentation Format`, 
    "Recalled Words ")) |> 
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

A factorial design

The Adler data set from the carData package comes from a study of experimenter expectancy effects (Adler, 1973), in a simplified version from Erickson and Nosanchuk (1977). Experimenters collected ratings of how successful people in photographs appeared to be. The photographs had been chosen because the people in them looked neither especially successful nor unsuccessful. Before collecting the data, the experimenters were told to expect either high or low ratings, and they were told to get good data, to get scientific data, or were given no such instruction. The outcome is the average success rating each experimenter obtained.

d_adler <- carData::Adler |>
  mutate(
    instruction = factor(
      instruction,
      levels = c("none", "good", "scientific"),
      labels = c("None", "Get Good Data", "Get Scientific Data")
    ),
    expectation = factor(
      expectation,
      levels = c("low", "high"),
      labels = c("Low Ratings", "High Ratings")
    )
  ) |>
  rename(
    Instruction = instruction,
    `Expected Ratings` = expectation,
    `Success Rating` = rating
  )
d_adler |> 
  ggplot(aes(`Expected Ratings` , `Success Rating`, color = `Expected Ratings`)) + 
  # geom_violin() +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, position = position_nudge(.15)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "text", aes(label = after_stat(y) |> signs::signs(accuracy = .1)), position = position_nudge(.25), hjust = 0, family = my_font, size = .8 * 14 / ggplot2::.pt) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(alpha = .5, pch = 16) + 
  theme_light(base_family = my_font, base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(begin = .2, end = .7) + 
  facet_grid(cols = vars(Instruction), labeller = "label_both") + 
  scale_y_continuous(labels = signs::signs)
Warning: Computation failed in `stat_summary()`.

The factorial model tests both main effects and their interaction. Interaction terms are labeled with a multiplication sign (e.g., Instruction × Expected Ratings).

fit_adler <- aov(`Success Rating` ~ Instruction * `Expected Ratings`, data = d_adler)
apa_anova(fit_adler)

Choosing columns

The anova_parameters argument selects the columns and their order. "Effect_Size" stands for whichever effect size is selected (see below), and "CI" adds its confidence interval. Columns are labeled by apa_anova automatically.

apa_anova(
  fit_adler,
  anova_parameters = c("Parameter", "df", "F", "p", "Effect_Size")
)

To mark significant effects, starred adds significance stars to a column, and bolded bolds the values of a column when the effect is significant. Columns are named as in anova_parameters (e.g., "Parameter" for the Source column).

apa_anova(fit_adler, starred = "F")

Effect Sizes

Choosing an effect size

By default, apa_anova displays partial eta squared (η2p), the most commonly reported effect size in psychology. Partial η2 is the proportion of variance explained by an effect after the variance explained by the other effects is set aside. Other effect sizes are available with the effect_size, partial, and generalized arguments:

Arguments Effect size
effect_size = "eta" (default) partial η2 (η2p)
effect_size = "eta", partial = FALSE η2
effect_size = "eta", generalized = TRUE generalized η2 (η2G)
effect_size = "omega" ω2p
effect_size = "omega", partial = FALSE partial ω2 (ω2p)
effect_size = "epsilon" partial ε2 (ε2p)
effect_size = NULL no effect size

η2 overestimates the population effect size in small samples. ω2 and ε2 are less biased, so they are good choices for small samples.

apa_anova(fit_adler, effect_size = "omega")

Generalized η2(Olejnik & Algina, 2003) is comparable across designs with different numbers of between- and within-subjects factors, which makes it useful for meta-analysis and for comparing studies. It is the default effect size in afex.

Confidence intervals

APA style recommends reporting confidence intervals for effect sizes. Add "CI" to anova_parameters to show them.

apa_anova(
  fit_adler,
  anova_parameters = c(
    "Parameter", "df", "F", "p", "Effect_Size", "CI"
  ),
  ci = 0.90
)

Intervals are two-sided. Because F tests are one-sided, a 90% interval is a natural companion to an F test with α = .05: the interval excludes 0 if and only if the F test is significant (Steiger, 2004). Its lower bound is 0 when the test is not significant. Set ci = 0.95 for 95% intervals.

Intervals are not shown for generalized η2, because the intervals computed by effectsize for it can exclude the point estimate. If you request them, apa_anova gives a warning and leaves them out.

Unbalanced Designs and Types of Sums of Squares

When cell sizes are unequal, the effects in a factorial design are correlated, and the sums of squares depend on how the variance they share is divided. In the Moore data set from the carData package, participants were paired with a partner of high or low status, and the number of times they conformed to their partner’s judgments was recorded. Participants’ authoritarianism was classified as low, medium, or high. The cell sizes are unequal:

d_moore <- carData::Moore |>
  mutate(
    fcategory = factor(fcategory, 
                       levels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
                       labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
    partner.status = factor(partner.status, 
                            levels = c("low", "high"),
                            labels = c("Low", "High"))
  ) |>
  rename(
    Authoritarianism = fcategory,
    `Authoritarianism Score` = fscore,
    `Partner Status` = partner.status
  )

table(d_moore$Authoritarianism, d_moore$`Partner Status`)

         Low High
  Low     10    5
  Medium   4   11
  High     8    7
d_moore |> 
  # rename(`Participant Authoritarianism` = Authoritarianism) |> 
  ggplot(aes(`Partner Status` , conformity, color = `Partner Status`)) + 
  # geom_violin() +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, position = position_nudge(.15)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "text", aes(label = after_stat(y) |> signs::signs(accuracy = .1)), position = position_nudge(.25), hjust = 0, family = my_font, size = .8 * 14 / ggplot2::.pt) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(alpha = .5, pch = 16) + 
  theme_light(base_family = my_font, base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(begin = .2, end = .7) + 
  facet_grid(cols = vars(`Authoritarianism`), labeller = "label_both") + 
  scale_y_continuous("Conformity", labels = signs::signs)

By default, apa_anova uses Type 1 (sequential) sums of squares, as anova and summary.aov do. Each effect is adjusted only for the effects entered before it, so the results depend on the order of the terms in the formula.

fit_moore <- lm(conformity ~ Authoritarianism * `Partner Status`, data = d_moore)
apa_anova(fit_moore)

Set type = 2 or type = 3 for Type 2 or Type 3 sums of squares, which are computed with car::Anova. Type 2 tests adjust each main effect for the other main effects but not for the interaction, which is appropriate when the interaction is negligible.

apa_anova(fit_moore, type = 2)

Type 3 tests adjust each effect for all other effects, including interactions. Type 3 tests are meaningful only when factors are coded with contrasts that sum to zero (e.g., contr.sum), not with R’s default treatment contrasts, so set the contrasts before fitting the model:

fit_moore_sum <- lm(
  conformity ~ Authoritarianism * `Partner Status`,
  data = d_moore,
  contrasts = list(Authoritarianism = contr.sum, `Partner Status` = contr.sum)
)
apa_anova(fit_moore_sum, type = 3)

A table from car::Anova or anova can also be passed to apa_anova directly. It already has a type of sums of squares, so the type argument is not needed.

car::Anova(fit_moore, type = 2) |>
  apa_anova()
apa_contrasts(fit_moore, contrast = `Partner Status`, by = Authoritarianism, effect_size = FALSE) |> 
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Analysis of Covariance

An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) is an ANOVA with one or more continuous covariates. Fit it with lm or aov. Here, partner status is tested while controlling for participants’ authoritarianism scores. Type 2 sums of squares adjust each effect for the other, regardless of the order of the terms.

fit_ancova <- lm(conformity ~ `Authoritarianism Score` + `Partner Status`, data = d_moore)
apa_anova(fit_ancova, type = 2)

Repeated-Measures Designs

Error strata with aov

In the obk.long data set from the afex package (O’Brien & Kaiser, 1985), 16 participants in three treatment groups were measured before treatment, after treatment, and at follow-up. Each phase had five measurements, which we average here.

d_obk <- obk.long |>
  mutate(phase = factor(phase, levels = c("pre", "post", "fup"))) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value), .by = c(id, treatment, phase)) |>
  rename(Treatment = treatment, Phase = phase)

In base R, a mixed design with a between-subjects factor (treatment) and a within-subjects factor (phase) is fit with aov and an Error term. Each error stratum has its own error term. apa_anova introduces each stratum with a heading row and indents its effects.

fit_obk_aov <- aov(value ~ Treatment * Phase + Error(id / Phase), data = d_obk)
apa_anova(fit_obk_aov)

With aov, sums of squares are Type 1, and no correction is made for violations of sphericity.

afex models

The afex package fits repeated-measures ANOVAs with Type 3 sums of squares and corrects the degrees of freedom of within-subjects effects for violations of sphericity (Greenhouse–Geisser by default). In afex models, each effect has its own error term, so the table shows the degrees of freedom of each effect and its error term (dfeffect and dferror) and the mean squared error (MSE), as afex’s nice function does. As in afex, generalized η2 is the default effect size.

fit_obk <- aov_ez(
  id = "id",
  dv = "value",
  data = d_obk,
  between = "Treatment",
  within = "Phase"
)
apa_anova(fit_obk)

The degrees of freedom of the within-subjects effects are not whole numbers because they have been corrected for sphericity. To report partial η2 with confidence intervals instead:

apa_anova(
  fit_obk,
  generalized = FALSE,
  anova_parameters = c(
    "Parameter", "df", "df_error", "F", "p", "Effect_Size", "CI"
  ),
  ci = 0.90
)

The sphericity correction is set when the model is fit or printed in afex (e.g., afex_options(correction_aov = "none")).

Linear mixed models

Repeated-measures ANOVAs need complete data from every participant, and they average over repeated measurements within each cell. Linear mixed models fit with lme4::lmer have neither requirement. Here the same O’Brien and Kaiser data are analyzed without averaging the five measurements within each phase, with a random intercept for each participant:

d_obk_trials <- obk.long |>
  mutate(phase = factor(phase, levels = c("pre", "post", "fup"))) |>
  rename(Treatment = treatment, Phase = phase)

fit_obk_lmer <- lme4::lmer(
  value ~ Treatment * Phase + (1 | id),
  data = d_obk_trials
)
apa_anova(fit_obk_lmer)

The F tests come from the lmerTest package, which must be installed. Models fit with lme4::lmer are converted for lmerTest automatically, and models fit with lmerTest::lmer are used as they are. Mixed models have no simple error terms, so each test’s denominator degrees of freedom (dferror) are approximated. By default, the approximation is Kenward–Roger’s (which requires the pbkrtest package), as in apa_parameters, so tables of the same model’s F tests and coefficients use the same approximation. Satterthwaite’s approximation, lmerTest’s default, is faster for large data sets:

tbl_obk_lmer <- apa_anova(fit_obk_lmer, ddf = "Satterthwaite")
apa_note(tbl_obk_lmer)
[1] "*F* tests of fixed effects are Type III. Denominator degrees of freedom are Satterthwaite approximations [@satterthwaiteApproximateDistributionEstimates1946]."

Tests are Type 3 by default, as in lmerTest. lmerTest’s Type 3 tests do not depend on how factors are coded, so sum-to-zero contrasts are not needed. Use type = 2 or type = 1 for other types.

Sums of squares and effect sizes have no agreed-upon definitions in mixed models, so they are not shown by default. When a partial effect size is requested, it is computed from F and its degrees of freedom (e.g., effectsize::F_to_eta2), and the note says that it only approximates the effect size:

apa_anova(
  fit_obk_lmer,
  effect_size = "eta",
  anova_parameters = c(
    "Parameter", "df", "df_error", "F", "p", "Effect_Size", "CI"
  )
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

ANOVA tables made by lmerTest’s anova function are displayed the same way, with the type of tests and the degrees-of-freedom method read from the table (e.g., apa_anova(anova(lmerTest_fit, type = 2))). Generalized linear mixed models (lme4::glmer) have no F tests. Use apa_parameters for them, as described in the multilevel article.

Customizing ANOVA Tables

Notes

The table does not say which type of sums of squares or which sphericity correction was used, so say so in a table note. apa_anova records how the table was made, and apa_note turns that record into note text:

tbl_moore <- apa_anova(fit_moore, type = 2)
apa_note(tbl_moore)
[1] "Type II sums of squares. *&eta;*^2^~p~ = partial eta squared."

The note says which type of sums of squares was used and defines the effect size. For afex models, it also says which effects have sphericity-corrected degrees of freedom. afex corrects only effects that involve a within-subjects factor with more than two levels, so the note names those factors:

tbl_obk <- apa_anova(fit_obk, starred = "F")
apa_note(tbl_obk)
[1] "Type III sums of squares. Degrees of freedom and *p*-values for effects involving Phase are Greenhouse–Geisser corrected [@greenhouseMethodsAnalysisProfile1959]. *MSE* = mean square error; *&eta;*^2^~G~ = generalized eta squared [@olejnikGeneralizedEtaOmega2003]. ^\\* ^*p* ≤ .05. ^\\*\\* ^*p* ≤ .01. ^\\*\\*\\* ^*p* ≤ .001."

When stars or bold values are used, the note explains them, after the general notes as APA style requires. The text is in markdown, and it does not start with “Note.” because apaquarto adds that.

With apaquarto, use apa_note in the apa-note chunk option with !expr. Chunk options are evaluated before the chunk runs, so make the table in an earlier chunk (as tbl_obk was made above) and display it in the chunk with the note. Write it as apa7::apa_note, because in documents with cached chunks, chunk options can be evaluated before library(apa7) takes effect:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-obk
#| tbl-cap: Mixed ANOVA of Treatment and Phase
#| apa-note: !expr apa7::apa_note(tbl_obk)
tbl_obk
```
Note. Type III sums of squares. Degrees of freedom and p-values for effects involving Phase are Greenhouse–Geisser corrected (Greenhouse & Geisser, 1959). MSE = mean square error; η2G = generalized eta squared (Olejnik & Algina, 2003). * p ≤ .05. ** p ≤ .01. *** p ≤ .001.

Without apaquarto, apa_flextable(tbl, note = TRUE) puts the same note below the table (or pass your own text as note). Do not combine it with the apa-note chunk option, or the note will appear twice.

The generated note is a starting point. To add to it, combine it with your own text (e.g., paste(apa_note(tbl_obk), "Outliers were removed.")). With collapse = NULL, apa_note returns one sentence per element, so you can drop or reword sentences.

apa_note reads an attribute of the table. dplyr functions such as mutate and filter keep it, but some operations (e.g., joins) drop it, so call apa_note on the table that apa_anova returned.

Labels and post-processing

Variable names are converted to title case (e.g., correct would become Correct). For better labels, rename the variables before fitting the model, as was done for the Moore data above. Because the output is a tibble, you can also change the labels afterward.

Further formatting is available with apa_flextable.

apa_anova(fit_adler) |>
  apa_flextable(table_width = .8)

Model comparisons

apa_anova makes source tables. To compare nested models (e.g., anova(m1, m2)), use apa_performance_comparison or pass a list of models to apa_parameters, as described in the regression article.

Using apa_parameters

apa_parameters returns the same table for aov and afex models, so apa_parameters(fit) and apa_anova(fit) are interchangeable for these models. To display the regression coefficients of an ANOVA model, fit it with lm and use apa_parameters. For linear mixed models, the two functions show different things: apa_anova tests each effect as a whole, and apa_parameters shows the fixed-effect coefficients and the random effects.
